The new Nobel laureate uses finely wrought forms to constrain a terrible excess of feeling.

By Merve Emre

Twice in the last five years, the Swedish Academy has awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature to a woman who takes eros seriously: Annie Ernaux, in 2022, and, now, Anne Carson. Each is, in her own way, a minimalist, and both have pursued forms of writing that constrain a terrible excess of feeling—that give shape and weight to the maelstrom of passion. Ἔρος δηὖτέ μ’ ὀ λυσιμέλης δόνει,
γλυκύπικρον ἀμάχανον ὄρπετον

Eros the melter of limbs (now again) stirs me—
sweetbitter unmanageable creature who steals in

I remember the “melter of limbs.” (Compare it to “loosener of limbs,” an ungainlier translation that makes Eros sound like a personal trainer.) I remember, too, the shock of “sweetbitter,” which sounded all wrong—perhaps because “bittersweet” was so familiar that it hid in plain sight the brutal simultaneity of pleasure and pain. Carson had used the familiar word for the title of her first book of criticism, “Eros the Bittersweet” (1986), about the ungovernable force of desire in ancient Greek literature. “Foreign to her will, it forces itself irresistibly upon her from without. Eros is an enemy,” she wrote. This enemy could be detained by a line of poetry, but it would always overrun the will’s defenses.

Translation is Carson’s primary art form. One way to describe it is as the art of sustained metaphor: a word in one language is similar, but not identical, to a word in another language. To translate is to commit to imperfection, to unlikeness and even error, from the get-go. “Aristotle says that metaphor causes the mind to experience itself / in the act of making a mistake,” Carson wrote in “Men in the Off Hours” (2000). “Not only that things are other than they seem, / and so we mistake them, / but that such mistakenness is valuable.” It is the mind’s experience of error and, through it, of discovery that courses through the rest of her writing, and that allows her to move among unlike things, whether within a line (“Eros shook my / mind like a mountain wind falling on oak trees,” from Sappho), or across an entire book, such as “Economy of the Unlost,” in which she reads Simonides of Keos as a distant analogue to Paul Celan, “a poet who uses language as if he were always translating.” The opposite of error is a kind of divine indifference—not bringing unlike things into considered proximity but strewing them about at random, and delighting in the disorder one creates. I think often of these chilling lines from “The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos” (2001):

What really connects words and things?

Not much, decided my husband
and proceeded to use language
in the way that Homer says the gods do.
All human words are known to the gods but have for them entirely other meanings
alongside our meanings.
They flip the switch at will.

My husband lied about everything.

We do not often come across people today who speak, as the Greek poets did, of desire, anger, grief, and pride. We hide our great passions under layers of compulsive, civilized talk. We ironize; we deflate. We are not minimalists; we minimize instead. In Carson’s poetry, the vehement language of an ancient tradition is placed side to side with the ordinary elements of modern life. The results can be comic and unexpectedly tender, like when the red-winged monster Geryon walks to his kindergarten classroom with his brother in “Autobiography of Red,” or the television scripts that feature Sappho, Antigone, and “Thucydides in Conversation with Virginia Woolf” in “Men in the Off Hours.” My favorite of Carson’s “Short Talks” (1992) is titled “Short Talk on the Sensation of Airplane Takeoff,” on the eros of commercial flight: “Well you know I wonder, it could be love running towards my life with its arms up yelling let’s buy it what a bargain!”

But eros is often tragic. This is its essential error. Love contains the seeds of its own destruction—the cruelty and self-absorption that turns the afflicted against one another, and themselves. Catullus told us as much in “Odi et Amo,” but I prefer the feral imagination of Carson’s “Plainwater” (1995): “Humans in love are terrible. no: tongue breaks and thin
fire is racing under skin
and in eyes no sight and drumming
fills ears

and cold sweat holds me and shaking
grips me all, greener than grass
I am and dead—or almost
I seem to me

Carson admires the absolute spiritual daring it takes to submit to one’s awful longings, and to find in this state a cold radiance, a “bleak exultation”—that is Emily Dickinson, another of Carson’s frequent references—that can look like either wisdom or madness. “What I like best about the three women we’ve been studying is that they know what love is,” she writes. “They know love is the touchstone of a true or a false spirituality.” Sappho supposedly threw herself off the Leucadian cliffs for the man she loved, unrequitedly. Dr. Haw says grief is a long process.
She frowns. What does it accomplish

all that raking up the past?
Oh—I spread my hands—
I prevail! I look her in the eye.
She grins. Yes you do. ♦

Moats! Does anyone have one anymore? As AI makes it easy to build anything, this is one of the biggest questions on people’s minds right now. Especially people trying to decide where to work. I teamed up with my frequent collaborator, the incredibly smart and insightful Dan Hockenmaier, to answer this question: How do I know if a given startup has a moat? The answer is a lot more interesting, and straightforward, than you’d expect. Let’s get into it.

There is a pervasive belief that startups are a lottery ticket. It’s impossible to pick winners, so it’s just a roll of the dice.

I couldn’t disagree more.

Not only can startups be a great learning experience and a lot of fun, but they can also provide economic rewards comparable to (or greater than) the “safe” route into big tech.

However, for this to be true, you must rigorously evaluate the startup you’re considering joining. Some of this is obvious: Does it have a strong team? Do customers love the product? Is it growing fast? But perhaps because it seems harder to measure, people often skip one of the most important criteria: Does it have a moat?

A company can check all your boxes and look like a rocket ship. If it doesn’t have a moat, though, it’s going to stall out. It won’t be able to keep growing once competition gets fierce, and it’s unlikely to reach a major liquidity event. That can mean wasting years of your life.

Moats are more important than ever in the AI era. Anyone can create a product; they can do it faster than ever before, and everyone is building the same things. But only some of these products will win.

Of course, assessing a startup’s moat isn’t an exact science. The good news is, there’s a simple framework that could meaningfully increase your odds of picking a winner or avoiding a flame-out, and you can apply it in just an hour after receiving an offer. The process will also teach you a lot about the business.

The framework has three steps:

  1. Identify a compounding advantage

  2. Gauge how strong that advantage could be

  3. Measure if it’s working

Step 1: Identify a compounding advantage

The first step is to figure out what kind of moat a startup could have. This can seem daunting, especially given how frenetic the conversation is on the topic right now. The term “moat” is being used much too loosely, as a stand-in for basically anything that gives a company an edge.

In reality, only a small subset of what people call moats actually drive the vast majority of long-term value.

They’re what I’ll call compounding advantages: not just a temporary edge, but a self-reinforcing flywheel that gets stronger and stronger over time, ultimately making a company very hard to compete with.

There are only four compounding advantages that really matter. Every major tech company has at least one. If you can’t see the potential for any in the startup you’re evaluating, that’s a red flag.

1. Switching costs: The more deeply embedded a product is in the way a customer works, the harder it is for that customer to switch. This increases retention and revenue per customer, which can be reinvested into the product.

2. Network effects: The more users a product has, the better it gets for everyone. This increases engagement and attracts more users.

3. Scale economies: The more volume a company has, the larger and more efficient its operations can be. This lowers unit costs, funding lower prices or a better product at the same price, further driving up volume.

4. Data effects: The more usage a product has, the more data it generates. This data can be used to improve the product and increase usage.

What about all of the other moats people talk about? Can they be compounding advantages as well?

A common one is speed of execution. It’s true that speed is critical for startups. But a company that has to sprint forever is not a good business. Ultimately, it will misstep, slow down, and competition will catch up. Speed gives a company more shots on goal as it tries to build a great product and a great business, but it must eventually find something more durable.

Another favorite is distribution. It does matter more than ever: building products has gotten easier, but getting them to customers has not. But distribution is not a compounding advantage either. It helps create the raw ingredients for one, but it is not one itself.

Finally, we have brand. The idea is that when everyone is building the same thing, the most resonant brand will win. But for startups, brand works more like customer acquisition spend: Put money in, get growth out. It’s not something that will effectively keep others from competing long-term. Brand can become a true compounding advantage (as with Coke or Nike or Apple), but it just takes too long to really matter for most startups.

Speed, distribution, brand, a great founding team, and lots of funding—these are all fuel. They get the car moving in the right direction. The four compounding advantages are what it looks like when the car starts rolling downhill on its own.

How to identify the compounding advantage

Your job is to identify which kind of compounding advantage a startup has the potential to build. It won’t be in full force yet (it takes a long time to develop), but it should be pretty clear which path they are on. That’s because it’s not something you can “bolt on”; it’s not some clever competitive tactic or a tweak you can make to your business model.

A compounding advantage is the core loop at the center of the business through which you add more value for customers. Defensibility emerges as a byproduct of turning the flywheel over and over.

So as you evaluate a company, don’t focus on what they say they are or what their “strategy” is. Focus on what they’re actually doing. What is the team working on every day? What’s on their roadmap? Which teams are large and influential inside the company?

Here is what to look for:

1. Switching costs

Switching costs are sometimes viewed negatively: as something that keeps customers trapped or a reason clunky legacy software never gets replaced.

But think about what it takes for a product to get into this position in the first place. It first has to become so deeply embedded into the way a customer works, so essential to their business, that they can’t remove it. That requires creating a product that delivers enormous value.

If you are building a venture-backed software company, I think the answer is once again “do it all.” Just build the whole thing—your moat is the totality of what you’ve built and completely owning the buying center.

Some have argued that AI is making switching costs irrelevant. AI does make the actual migration faster and cheaper, but that is not where most switching costs actually come from. The bigger cost is what I’ll call the “workflow tax”: all of the time the team spends learning a product and building it into how they work, and how disruptive it is to do that over again. AI also helps teams build products much faster, which could allow them to become even more embedded across a wider range of surfaces.

At the core of these companies is a machine to both deepen and broaden customer engagement. The roadmap is rich with efforts to better serve existing use cases or create ways to serve new ones. They’ll often be focused on integrations and working with other parts of their customers’ stack. The team should be heavily tilted toward product and engineering, with an emphasis on shipping rapidly.

The classic examples are large incumbents with broad, deeply embedded products in SaaS, fintech, and healthcare, like Salesforce, Datadog, ADP, and Epic. But there are many earlier-stage companies that are currently on a path to creating something similar.

Rippling is a great example. Parker Conrad is building what he calls a “compound startup.” They started with employee onboarding and expanded rapidly across HR services, talent, finance, payroll, and business intelligence, all operating on shared infrastructure. This is the kind of product that gets embedded so deeply it rarely gets ripped out.

Network-effect businesses are totally different—so different, in fact, that most product features and the UI itself matter very little. How is it that Craigslist can still get so much traffic when it looks like this, in 2026?

Because what matters most is the network. The value of a network-effect business increases with each additional user. It’s all about having all of the people customers want to interact with, all of the content they want to consume, or all of the products they want to buy.

Network-effect products are common in industries like social (LinkedIn), gaming (Roblox), and marketplaces (Amazon).

The emphasis of a network business is less on building out the surface area or feature set of the product, and more on growing the network and making it easier and easier for that network to interact.

For example, during my years at Faire (a marketplace connecting local retailers and independent brands), the vast majority of our roadmap was focused on just a few things:

  1. Getting more retailers

  2. Getting more brands and making sure we had all of their products

  3. Improving the search and discovery algorithm to recommend the right products

  4. Reducing risk so retailers could try more products (free shipping, net terms, bigger credit limits)

Every decision gets filtered through one lens: “Does this strengthen the network?”

Businesses with scale as their compounding advantage are all about making it possible to offer the same product at a lower cost or a higher-quality product at the same cost.

These businesses are often highly capital-intensive: They make a big investment, such as in a production facility, warehouse, or LLM training run, and figure out how to get it to pay back. And then they do it again, but this time try to do it bigger and faster.

They’ll often have larger operations, engineering, and finance teams. And they will usually be focused on expansion: into newer, higher-scale operations and into new geographies and categories. Scale businesses are commonly found in industries like manufacturing (SpaceX), retail (Costco), media (Netflix), and now in the frontier labs.

Zipline (the autonomous delivery robot company) is a good example of a startup where scale economies are starting to emerge. They benefit from scale in two ways: by manufacturing more drones to reduce unit costs and by increasing delivery density to improve their utilization rate. The result is a cost per delivery that has fallen from $300 at launch to $12 today. Anyone who wants to compete with them will first have to go through the expensive part of that curve.

4. Data effects

The final type of compounding advantage has historically been relatively rare, but AI is making it much more common.

These are businesses with data at the core. It’s the input that makes the product higher-quality, more efficient, or work for more use cases. And by using the product, customers generate even more data, which further compounds this effect.

In these companies, you’ll often see a large effort to collect and sanitize data, and to build algorithms and products on top of it. ML and data science are usually large and influential teams.

One good example is Stripe Radar. They use transaction data across all merchants to get better at detecting fraud for each of them. Stripe has processed over 70 trillion data points and $1.9 trillion in transaction volume. 92% of all transactions use a card it has seen before. The result is a product that a company with access to less data can’t match.

Many AI products have the potential for this compounding advantage because of how much they can be improved with more data. Cursor is a clear example: with each accept or reject from users, the model gets better at understanding what good code looks like. Steven Pinker and Scott Alexander have stumbled into a public debate about existential AI risk. Alexander exploded at Pinker on twitter/X for being consistently dismissive of doomers, like him. He angrily challenged Pinker to an in-person debate, with money on the winner. Pinker didn’t rise to this on twitter but instead published an open letter to Alexander, setting out his case against doomerism. His tone was conciliatory and impeccably civil. Alexander has now replied with a long - very long - post in which he takes Pinker to task for what he perceives to be the shallowness of his arguments, ignorance of the relevant literature, and arrogant dismissal of doomers.

I am not going to get into the content of the debate here, because I want to see it play out first. But I will say something about the different styles of debating employed by the participants. In contrast to Pinker, Alexander, in his article, is pugnacious, petulant, and personal. Pinker tried to take the heat out of the exchange; Alexander turned it up again. He’s received a lot of criticism for this. I have to say, I liked it. I found Pinker’s cool, eminently reasonable style a little unsatisfying, and I’m glad Alexander didn’t feel the need to adopt it.

Let’s remember, they are arguing about whether there is a significant chance our species could be destroyed by its own invention. That seems like something worth getting emotional about. The dryness with which doomers sometimes discuss such possibilities makes them sound mad rather than reasonable. More generally, a satisfying public debate should have a little spice, some electrical charge, even a little irrationality. Not just because that makes it more entertaining for the rest of us, but because it signals there is something at stake beyond victory or defeat in an intellectual game.

It also feels more honest. When you see what makes someone passionate or frustrated or annoyed you’re getting to see who they are and what they care about. Debaters who hide all unruly emotion behind a smooth veneer of civility can seem remote and inscrutable, and difficult to trust. (To be clear, I’m talking about marginal cases like this one, where both participants grasp the essentials of meaningful argument. I’m well aware that our public discourse doesn’t exactly suffer from an excess of civility or a deficit of emotion.)

Get your petty insecurities out on the table, I say. That’s certainly what Alexander does. In his article, responding to the tweet, Pinker joked about duelling, and said that Alexander writes “as if you are defending your honour”. He assured him, genially, that there is no need for this (honour being a concept alien to most intellectual debates, after all). But in his response, Alexander picked up on this theme and said, yes, actually, this is about honour:

I agree that in-person debates are confrontational and bad for truth-seeking. But I didn’t propose a debate in order to seek truth. I proposed it because, under California Penal Code § 415(1), it’s illegal for me to challenge you to a duel. I think your public writing on this topic has been dishonorable. Out of obligation, I will respond to the meaty arguments that you have set out for me. But what would be viscerally satisfying would be to make you get up on a stage where I read your own words to you in real time and ask “Really? Really?” after each sentence. Then I could watch you squirm as you try to square your output with your status as one of America’s top public intellectuals.

Some people have been appalled by this passage. It’s obvious to me that he’s joking (no, I don’t think Alexander is literally threatening violence). On the other hand, he is also serious. He’s being transparent about how he feels about the way Pinker has engaged - or not - with him and his school of thinkers. That isn’t merely petty; it is an oblique way of saying that Pinker ought to care more about this question than he does.

Emotion can be the enemy of clear thinking, but it can also be its friend. Recall that David Hume didn’t just say that “reason is the slave of the passions”; he said that it is and ought only to be. The passions tell us what to use our powers of reason on in the first place.

Emotions also motivate us to put more effort into our thinking. The Alexander-Pinker exchange bears this out, so far. On the substance of this issue I lean to Pinker’s side but I found his arguments a little shallow and unconvincing. Alexander’s are more detailed, nuanced and thought-through (and while he goes over the top in his parsing of Pinker’s previous statements, he does score some palpable hits there, as when he exposes Pinker’s misreading of the RAND report).

I would say that Alexander’s piece is a better piece of writing, even though it is over-long and overwrought. Pinker is a fine writer but Alexander is a master at combining clarity of exposition with antic wit and ‘voice’. When he takes the reader through complicated concepts you never feel like you’re reading a neutral explainer. He’s always fully present. For all that he’s a tech rationalist, his prose is more richly human than the more elegant Pinkerian style.

Does this mean I agree with Alexander on AI risk? No, not yet anyway. It’s more that Pinker came across as complacent to me. In Round Two, I hope to see him stoop to Alexander’s level and raise his game.

Allereerst: welkom alle nieuwe inschrijvers en volgers! In deze nieuwsbrief deel ik elke week (of elke twee weken) een inzicht uit de psychologie, een column, een podcast of nieuws over een boek. In dit geval: de deep dive in het werk van Jean Piaget die we deden met de podcast Normale Mensen Bestaan Niet. We maakten twee afleveringen, waar ik stiekem best trots op ben.

We zien de wereld niet zoals de wereld is. We zien de wereld zoals wij zijn. Of specifieker: om de wereld te begrijpen maken we er een kaart van in ons hoofd. Die kaart passen we voortdurend aan met nieuwe informatie, en we gebruiken die kaart om door de wereld te navigeren. Hoe meer we over de wereld weten, hoe gedetailleerder de kaart. Het bouwen van die kaarten begint in onze (vroege) jeugd.

Met Normale Mensen Bestaan Niet - de podcast die ik maak met Lennard Toma - maakten we een dubbelaflevering over het werk van Jean Piaget (1896 - 1980). Piaget was Zwitser, studeerde onder Carl Jung en was de grondlegger van de (cognitieve) ontwikkelingspsychologie. En hij was briljant. Nee maar écht. Dat bleek bijvoorbeeld uit dat hij op zijn tiende al een baan aangeboden kreeg als curator in een wetenschappelijk museum. Het was de prijs die hij won in een wedstrijd voor wetenschappelijke essays, hij stuurde een tractaat in over het paringsgedrag van slakken. Hij moest de baan afslaan, want het mocht niet van zijn ouders.

Piaget ging studeren en besloot zijn leven te besteden aan de filosofie. In het bijzonder vond hij kentheorie interessant, de tak van de filosofie die zich bezig houdt met hoe we onze kennis over de wereld opdoen. Om écht te begrijpen hoe we leren over de wereld, besloot hij onderzoek te doen naar degenen onder ons die daar het meest mee bezig zijn: kinderen. Hij dacht in eerste instantie een paar jaar te gaan besteden met dat uitstapje naar de ontwikkelingspsychologie, maar zou er zijn leven lang mee bezig blijven.

Piaget wilde erachter komen hoe kinderen leren over de wereld. Hij gebruikte daartoe een voor die tijd revolutionaire onderzoeksmethode: hij práátte met de kinderen. Zo kwam hij erachter dat de ontwikkeling van kinderen in een aantal verschillende fases verloopt, waarin het kind steeds nieuwe informatie leert op het niveau waarop het dat aankan. Piaget is nog steeds de meest invloedrijke denker in de ontwikkelingspsychologie (al wordt inmiddels niet meer gedacht dat zijn ontwikkelfases heilig zijn). Piaget is tot op de dag van vandaag relevant, niet alleen omdat hij ons inzicht geeft in hoe kinderen leren, maar ook omdat we daarmee beter kunnen begrijpen hoe we als volwassenen de wereld begrijpen.

In de podcast (hieronder linkjes!) bespreken Len en ik het werk van Piaget in twee afleveringen. Hieronder alvast onze grootste inzichten:

  1. De wereld leren begrijpen is een actief proces

Kennis over de wereld vergaar je niet zomaar, daar moet je een hoop voor doen. Nu zul je denken, ja héhé. Maar toch is een groot deel van ons onderwijssysteem gebouwd op het idee dat kinderen vooral passieve informatie-ontvangers zijn. Zitten en luisteren naar feiten en informatie, dat is volgens Piaget niet hoe je leert over de wereld. Volgens Piaget zijn kinderen ‘kleine wetenschappers’, die onderzoek doen in de wereld. Ze doen observaties (‘dit knopje zet het licht aan en uit!’), stellen op basis daarvan experimenten op (‘als ik heel vaak dit lichtknopje omzet, wordt mama dan boos?’) en gebruiken de onderzoeksdata die ze zo opdoen in beter en meer begrip over de wereld. Je leert dus het best over de wereld door ermee te interacteren, te spelen, te ontdekken en van je fouten te leren. Het liefst elke dag.

  1. Ons begrip van de wereld gaat via cognitieve schema’s

We kunnen de wereld niet als geheel snappen, daar is ‘ie simpelweg te complex voor. Dus wat we doen is in ons hoofd een representatie maken van de wereld. Een kaart, zo je wil, of in de taal van Piaget een schema. In zo’n schema staat alle informatie die je nodig hebt. Je hebt bijvoorbeeld een schema van een tafel, en dat betekent dat je wanneer je een kamer binnenloopt en je ziet een tafel, die meteen kunt gebruiken. Je hoeft niet eerst te kijken wat dat voor raar ding is, of de handleiding te lezen. Je begrip van een tafel gaat vooraf aan je interactie met dat stukje wereld.

Een kind (en een volwassene trouwens ook) leert over de wereld door er in het hoofd cognitieve schema’s van te maken. Die schema’s worden voortdurend geüpdate en aangepast - een proces dat Piaget adaptatie noemde. Leert een kind iets nieuws over de wereld dat nog niet in dat schema besloten ligt (‘een huis is niet alleen een gebouw met een een puntdak, maar kan ook een plat dak hebben’), dan wordt het bestaande schema bijgewerkt - geassimileerd. Past de nieuwe informatie niet meer in het oude schema (‘dit gebouw is geen huis, maar een kantoor’), dan moet een nieuw schema worden gemaakt - accomodatie.

Volgens Piaget moeten assimilatie en accommodatie wel een beetje in balans zijn. Te veel kennis kunnen inpassen in bestaande schema’s is te weinig uitdagend en dus saai. Maar de hele tijd volledig nieuwe informatie vinden die je bestaande begrip van de wereld te buiten gaan is desoriënterend en overdonderend.

  1. Een kind leert over de wereld op het eigen cognitieve niveau

Een kind leert zo over de wereld op het cognitieve niveau dat het heeft. Hoe ouder het kind, hoe complexer de schema’s. Dit begrip van de wereld wordt beperkt door de fysieke en neurologische ontwikkeling van het kind. In de eerste fase (0-2) ontstaan de eerste basale schema’s (ik vs niet-ik / mama / papa). Het kind leert door de wereld te manipuleren, door met dingen in de wereld te spelen en bijvoorbeeld door dingen in de mond te stoppen. In de volgende fase (3-7) bouwt het al flink wat schema’s op, maar moet kennis nog wel letterlijk en direct observeerbaar zijn. In de fases daarna (8-11 en 12-verder) komt er steeds meer ruimte voor abstract redeneren en symbolisch en hypothetisch denken. Belangrijk is dus vooral dat kinderen informatie aangeboden krijgen op het niveau dat passend is - anders is het simpelweg niet in te passen in hun cognitieve schema’s.

And it’s also a city where history is literally everywhere you look. Spend a week in Vienna and you will experience both time moving forward at great speed and time stood still in many places.

My first longer stay in Vienna was in 1977 and 1978 when my father was posted there for the first time and I remember a grey and drab city at the edge of Europe, West in terms of liberties, East in many other aspects, but mostly very self absorbed, moody and unfriendly to foreigners. I saw Vienna develop into the wonderful, modern, open, vibrant and attractive, colourful city it is today. Without moving, it went from the edge of free Europe to the very heart of it. That made all the difference.

My fascination for this rather radical change is not shared by many, certainly not by all the Viennese. Perhaps because in some ways it’s also a form of restoration. In less than a century first capital of a huge multinational and multicultural empire; capital of a newly established republic after military defeat and collapse of the empire; major city in the German Reich; capital of a quasi occupied, soviet dominated nation; capital of a nation that regained its liberty under strict conditions of eternal neutrality; capital of one of the most successful EU member states. One and the same city in so many different guises. For some Viennese all of this happened in their lifetime.

When emperor Franz Joseph died in 1916, my paternal grandparents were 13 years old. My grandfather once told me his first conscious news memory was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo. If that doesn’t impress you much, look up the filmed interview with Bertrand Russell in 1952, where he shares his memories of his grandfather - who raised him, because he lost his parents in early infancy - who travelled to Elba to meet Napoleon.

The point I’m trying to make is that if we want to live with history, as opposed to living in history, which is a form of sterile nostalgia, we have to be aware of the tectonic shifts in history that can occur in one or two lifetimes, sometimes even quicker, in a matter of years. Worlds deemed unmovable can completely disappear overnight. Also in an interview in 1960 Russel emphasised the changes that occurred between his birth in 1872 and his old age. The world he lived in as an old man would be totally incomprehensible to his grandfather a century before. For the British ruling classes at the end of the nineteenth century, the empire was eternal with Britain ruling the waves forever. The continent was of no great concern, although France needed to be mistrusted and Germany admired, even if Bismarck was seen as a peasant and a parvenu. Germany could become a rival on land, but never at sea, but since Britain had no interest in what happened on the continent and the Germans giving the French a good thrashing from time to time was not a bad thing, who cares? (Russell quotes Bismarck in saying that Britain is a whale and Germany an elephant, both the biggest beast in their own habitat, but never rivals).

What happens if the world changes so fast and you are still stuck in the old world when trying to cope with the challenges of the new world? Well, I guess you will be prone to make mistakes. The shock of change can be brutal. The speed with which the Industrial Revolution and the dawn of the oil based economy occurred at the end of the nineteenth century was impossible to keep up with mentally, emotionally, politically, institutionally. An orgy of riches that seemed to be endless, hubris without limits, upending a century that had already seen so much upheaval. It all culminated in the Great War, the beginning of Europe’s repeated attempts at collective suicide. That is where Europe caught up with the profound effects of the Industrial Revolution, that is where the ideologies were born that would make tens of millions of victims in less than half a century, ideologies that linger on and sometimes attempt a revival to this day.

Bertrand Russell refused to fight in the Great War, a decision that cost him his tenure in Cambridge and landed him in prison. For him the war was unnecessary and unjustified. A generation later he would defend fighting against Hitler. Some wars are justified.

Joseph Roth volunteered to fight in the Great War. Fin de siècle hubris was part of it, perhaps also the influence of romanticism, depicting war as an act of chivalry. It is this combination of carelessness and callousness on the factory floor first and the battle field after that set the stage for the parade of thugs and mass murderers like Mussolini, Stalin and Hitler who would lead Europe into the second phase of attempted collective suicide.

My fascination for the study of history grows with every year I live and work. It helps me understand never to exclude the unthinkable and never to assume things are inevitable. Was the Great War inevitable? I can’t see why. But once it happened, things were set in motion that led to literally unimaginable acts of genocide ten, twenty, twenty five years later.

As a student I was told by very smart professors that German reunification would never happen. A mere four years before it actually happened. And most could not imagine the end goal of the vision Putin developed over the years, inspired by the likes of Ivan Ilyin and other romantic reactionaries, who dreamt up a Russian empire that would neither be totalitarian, nor democratic.

Since Peter the Great, European nations have made the same mistake with Russia. Assuming that Russia’s ardent wish to be seen as a ‘civilised country’; its efforts to contribute to and integrate into European culture; its Europeanised elites; its huge investment in European architecture, industry, defence, would also entail its adoption of European values, European ways of life. A tragic mistake.

Russia under the old regime, under the communists obviously, but also under the new regime, is a “patrimonial” state, as professor Samuel Pipes called it. Which means that ultimate and absolute power and control, including over any form of property, resides with the boss, be that the Czar, the Secretary-General of the CPSU or the Russian president. Since all things copied from the West have the tendency to stimulate personal freedoms, the patrimonial state can only keep things under control with repression. Not even two revolutions changed that. And Putin was prepared to give up on all highly needed economic reforms years ago just to have enough money to increase repression and implement Ilyin’s vision of a militarised Russian empire.

The tragedy of Russia is that rulers are ultimately brought down because the financial, economic, social and human cost of repression prevents them from implementing reforms that are necessary for their very survival. Both the Czars and the communists tried and failed, leading to unspeakable misery for the Russian people. Putin’s adventurism can be seen as an attempt to avoid the same fate.

Our duty is to see Russia as it is and not as we would like it to be. There has been too much wishful thinking and acting, frankly on both sides of the argument. Once Putin’s Waterloo has run its course, which sadly even after five years of bloodshed in Ukraine will probably still take considerable time, we will have to define how we want to relate to our problematic neighbour in the east.

By now it is clear Putin failed. Not just the usual “I tried but it didn’t work out”. He failed in such an epic way that he took his nation to the deepest and darkest pits of moral corruption. For it is not the creation of a class of obscenely rich oligarchs who were allowed to plunder the nation’s riches that defines Putin’s poison best, nor the utterly corrupt state structures, nor the killing of anyone who opposes him, not even the orgies of war crimes in Chechnya, Syria and Ukraine. No, it’s the moral corruption he has created where all the above is justified in moral, even Christian terms, where cruelty, racism, gender based violence, the witch hunt of gays have all become part of state ideology and have corrupted the so often hailed “Russian soul”.

It is this corruption that allows Putin to send hundreds of thousands of young men into battle, untrained, unequipped, barely armed, barely fed, barely clothed, to die as cannon fodder. It is this corruption that allows him to send bands of thugs into Ukraine to rape women and girls, to abduct children, to loot and destroy all they encounter.

This is only possible because the people have been fed lies for so long that they believe Putin’s narrative or are confused enough not to doubt it or afraid enough not to challenge it. It’s not a first. It’s happened many times before in many places. And it’s happening in quite a number of places today. Once the media are under control, the narrative is under control and the brainwashing can begin. Give people a reason to be resentful, give them a reason to be afraid, give them someone to blame, then to hate and you are two steps away from violence. Anywhere. This is not just a Russian problem. Just take a look at the range of politicians who over the years copied Putin’s playbook. Not all of them succeeded. But not enough of them failed. And this should give us pause to think.

The fall of the Berlin Wall was the first “Zeitenwende” since WW2. The invasion of Ukraine is the second. The latter is a consequence of the first, since Russia saw itself as the only looser at the end of the Cold War, and Putin’s politics of revanchism and restoration of Russia’s grandeur was built on that sentiment. As long as I can remember political speeches are filled with references to “crossroads”. Apparently we are permanently moving from one historical crossroads to the next. Nonsense. Politics is about making choices, on a daily basis. All too often politicians try to sell any decision as historic. Sure, many decisions and many events can be qualified as historic. The murder of empress Elisabeth of Austria in Geneva in 1898 is a historic event. But it did not change the course of history. It was another murder, sixteen years later in Sarajevo that did the trick by triggering a Zeitenwende. So there are many events that become historic and some that change the course of history. It’s the latter that should get more attention from policy makers. The ability to distinguish between the two can make all the difference between failure and success in policy making. Drawing the wrong conclusion can have tragic long term consequences. One only has to remember the historic mistake of the invasion of Iraq after 9/11, to understand what I mean.

If Putin’s invasion of Ukraine signals a “Zeitenwende”, what are the conclusions that need to be drawn? First and foremost that Putin cannot be allowed to win, because his victory would be the first step towards the undoing of all the gains for Europe and its nations since the end of the European divide. Second is the realisation that the transatlantic security relationship is of existential importance to Europe, more so than to the US. Trump’s administration turning against its allies and siding with Putin could become another ‘Zeitenwende’ if it is not corrected. And even if it is, trust between the US on the one hand and Europe and Canada on the other was damaged permanently. What was done by Trump, can be done again and Europe needs to prepare for that. Which means that the nature of European integration has to change to speed up the accession of new members, Ukraine first and foremost. So Ukraine has to be included in all the transformational projects Europe is now putting into place to build up the necessary military-industrial capabilities, to speed up the energy transition to create European energy sovereignty, to face the climate crisis and the challenges linked to AI and other aspects of today’s Industrial Revolution. Before the rise of the extreme right in places like Germany creates another ‘Zeitenwende’, Putin’s followers and copycats in our own nations and the ideology they propagate need to be confronted and challenged head on, lest this poison not take hold in large parts of our society. Which means addressing the root causes of people’s dissatisfaction, linked to socio-economic injustice and social-cultural insecurity.

Ten years after the end of WW2, Romy Schneider brought empress Elisabeth back to life on the big screen. The Sissi trilogy creates a fairytale world of glamour, love, order and a Germanic “Heimat” untainted by nazis and the moral depravity with which they infected the whole society. It was, if you wish, the cultural and social pendant of the “Wirtschaftswunder”.

Just what the doctor ordered for a society desperate to recreate some moral order. So why are we now bombarded with films, documentaries, books, tv series about Sissi? Are we looking for a feminist icon or is it nostalgia for a society when everything seemed set in stone and everyone knew their place? Or a bit of both?

History will always come into play when we are trying to make sense of where we are in time and where we are going. We need references, things and people to relate to, to admire or to be horrified by. History and narratives can inoculate us against the risk of becoming prisoners of the here and now and thus blind for the expressions of brilliance and of horror, which are both part of human nature. And it can help us distinguish between events, historic events and historic turning points. Knowing you are at a turning point is a good start, but not more than that. Being able to act, to have the audacity to question your assumptions, to respond to transformative times with transformative policies, will be the true measure of leadership and could determine the difference between failure and success. It is the interaction between (long term) developments, events and political decisions that will set the course of history. Scary, perhaps, but certainly also motivating and inspiring.

Ik voel zijn afwezigheid elke dag, ondanks dat we elkaar, toen hij nog leefde, niet elke dag spraken.

Toen mijn vriend zo onverwacht wegviel, heb ik veel geschreven over wie hij voor mij was. Ik merk dat alles wat ik schreef te klein was. Ik heb dat trouwens ook naar enkele dierbare vrienden en vriendinnen uitgesproken, dat ik geen taal heb voor onze vriendschap, zo waardevol.

Luisteren met Levinas is een door lezers gesteunde publicatie. Wil je nieuwe posts ontvangen en mijn werk steunen? Overweeg dan om gratis of betalende abonnee te worden.

Hij kwam als ik hulp nodig had. Hij moedigde me aan op speciale momenten. Hij was er gewoon, zonder uitnodiging. Wil je even luisteren, dat hoefde ik hem niet te vragen. Hij had al gehoord wat ik niet zei.

Voor mij heeft vriendschap naarmate ik ouder werd meer te maken gekregen met ruimte: verbonden zijn zonder verwachtingen; weten dat iemand er is zonder voortdurend iets te hoeven vragen of teruggeven. De vriendschappen die mij het dierbaarst zijn, laten het woord nabijheid vrij ademen. Ik heb gemerkt dat die vriendschappen blijven, ook als het lang stil blijft. En als we elkaar weer zien, luisteren we gewoon naar wat er is. Dat is zo belangrijk voor mij.

Twee bijzinnen

Michel de Montaigne (1533–1592) was een Franse schrijver en denker uit de streek rond Bordeaux. Daar, waar hij als jurist werkte, leerde hij Étienne de La Boétie kennen. Later trok hij zich terug in een toren op zijn landgoed en begon hij met schrijven. Montaigne onderzocht al schrijvend wat hij dacht, en gebruikte zichzelf daarbij als materiaal. Zijn vriend stierf in 1563, op tweeëndertigjarige leeftijd.

Toen Montaigne wilde uitleggen waarom hij zoveel van Étienne de La Boétie had gehouden, bleef hij steken bij een korte zin. Hij schreef hem in de marge van zijn eigen exemplaar van de Essais, volgens de overlevering in twee keer: eerst de ene helft, later, met andere inkt, de tweede. Parce que c’estoit luy, parce que c’estoit moy (omdat hij het was, omdat ik het was). La Boétie was toen al jaren dood. Hun vriendschap had maar een paar jaar geduurd. Wat Montaigne erover kon zeggen, paste dus in die twee bijzinnen.

Ik lees die zin graag: Omdat hij het was. Omdat ik het was. Meer lijkt hij niet te zeggen, en daardoor blijft alles open. Sinds drie jaar lees ik de zin ook als de woorden van mezelf, ik die ben achtergebleven.

Elders in hetzelfde essay beschrijft Montaigne hoe de zielen van twee vrienden zich zo vermengen dat de grens tussen hen verdwijnt. Dat beeld van vermengen heeft een lange geschiedenis. Aristoteles noemde de vriend allos autos (een ander zelf): iemand in wie ik het goede herken dat ik ook in mijzelf zoek. Ware vriendschap bestaat volgens hem tussen mensen die op elkaar lijken in deugd, en ze vraagt om wederkerigheid. Beide vrienden willen het goede voor de ander, en ze weten dat van elkaar.

Dat is voor mij heel herkenbaar. Een vriendin is vaak iemand bij wie je niet steeds opnieuw hoeft te beginnen, die als ze een halve zin hoort, weet wat er onder ligt. Bij zo iemand hoeft je niet de hele tijd te werken. In vriendschap is er rust, omdat een deel van de uitleg wegvalt.

Hannah Arendt

In haar essay over Lessing, opgenomen in Men in Dark Times, schrijft zij over vriendschap als een verhouding waarin mensen met elkaar spreken over de wereld. Bij haar opent vriendschap zich naar buiten. Het is voor haar een manier om de wereld bewoonbaar te houden, en tussen vrienden ontstaat een ruimte waarin dingen gezegd en herzien kunnen worden. Zo helpt een vriendin mij de wereld te verdragen die groter is dan ik.

Dat vind ik een mooie gedachte. Wie alleen naar de wereld kijkt, vindt haar al snel te hard of te vreemd. Vrienden blijven met ons spreken, soms zacht en soms met een zin die pas dagen later aankomt. Mijn vriendinnen geven mij daarbij lang niet altijd gelijk.

le Même

Als je Levinas leest, voel ik bij het beeld van vriendschap als herkenning toch een ongemak opkomen. Bij Levinas is de verhouding tot de Ander asymmetrisch. De Ander komt van elders, uit een hoogte die ik niet kan inhalen, en laat zich daarom slecht denken als tweede exemplaar van mijzelf. Waar ik mijzelf herken in een ander, ben ik al snel bezig met wat Levinas le Même (het Zelfde) noemt: de beweging waarin alles wat ik tegenkom wordt teruggebracht tot iets wat ik al ken.

Bij een vriend gebeurt dat bijna ongemerkt. Ik denk: zo is zij. Ik hoor aan haar stem wat er aan de hand is. Vaak klopt dat ook, en vriendschap ‘leeft’ van deze energie. Toch schuilt daar ook wel een gevaar. Hoe beter mijn beeld van de ander lijkt te kloppen, hoe minder ik nog verwacht dat zij mij kan verrassen. Dan wordt vertrouwdheid een stille vorm van bezit.

Luisteren naar een vriend lijkt eenvoudig, omdat ik zoveel al weet. Toch vermoed ik dat luisteren in vriendschap een van de moeilijkste vormen van aandacht is. Bij een vreemde weet ik dat ik nog niets weet. Bij een vriendin vergeet ik dat. Ik hoor haar door mijn herinneringen heen, en ik hoor de oude versie van haar, terwijl zij intussen ergens anders is aangekomen.

Sera Knight

Levinas heeft dit bezwaar scherp geformuleerd in zijn teksten over Martin Buber. Buber beschreef de ontmoeting tussen Ik en Jij als een wederzijdse relatie, en Levinas had grote waardering voor dat denken. Toch vond hij die wederkerigheid te licht, te etherisch. Hij stelde daar iets tastbaars tegenover: de Ander die honger heeft en gevoed wil worden, die het koud heeft en kleding nodig heeft. Bij Levinas begint verantwoordelijkheid bij het lichaam van de Ander en bij het brood dat ik uit mijn eigen mond haal om te geven.

Dat klinkt echt heel groot, voor een leuk contact zeker te groot. Maar ik herken er wel iets in. Een vriend is iemand met wie ik diep praat, en ook iemand voor wie ik de telefoon opneem als ik moe ben, of voor wie ik soep maak. Ik vraag haar of ze goed is thuisgekomen en of ze vandaag heeft gegeten. Vriendschap wordt werkelijk in wat je voor elkaar doet: tijd, aandacht, zorg, wachten, praktische trouw.

Boekhouding

In een gesprek met Philippe Nemo, later gebundeld als Éthique et infini (Ethiek en oneindigheid), zei Levinas dat wederkerigheid de zaak van de Ander is. Ik ben verantwoordelijk zonder te wachten op wat de Ander voor mij doet. Ik schrik terug van vriendschappen waarin stilletjes wordt bijgehouden wie het laatst belde en wie het vaakst gaf. Levinas legt die vraag bij mij terug: houd ik zelf ergens zo’n boekhouding bij? Soms beschermt zo’n rekening iemand ook, want er zijn vriendschappen waarin iemand leegloopt.

Opvallend genoeg zit er bij Aristoteles een barst in het symmetrische beeld. In het achtste boek van de Ethica Nicomachea schrijft hij dat vriendschap meer bestaat in liefhebben dan in bemind worden. Als voorbeeld noemt hij moeders die hun kind liefhebben terwijl dat kind hen nog niets teruggeeft. Jacques Derrida heeft die passage in Politiques de l’amitié (Politiek van de vriendschap) uitvoerig gelezen. In de traditie die de vriend als gelijke denkt, klinkt dus ook een stem die het zwaartepunt legt bij degene die liefheeft, los van wat er terugkomt.

Het scherpste punt dat Levinas voor vriendschap oplevert, ligt voor mij bij het kennen. Vrienden kennen elkaar vaak lang. Ik hoor aan één korte zin wat eronder ligt, en ik ken haar aarzelingen en haar manier van wegkijken. Daar leeft vriendschap van, en daar is zij ook kwetsbaar.

In Totalité et Infini (Totaliteit en Oneindig) beschrijft Levinas le visage (het Gelaat) als de wijze waarop de Ander zich aandient en tegelijk de voorstelling die ik van hem heb te buiten gaat. Bij een vriend vergeet ik dat het snelst, omdat mijn beeld zo goed lijkt te kloppen. Ik denk dat ik haar begrijp, terwijl ik vooral mijn geschiedenis met haar begrijp. Ik hoor haar vandaag door alles heen wat zij vorig jaar of tien jaar geleden was.

Niet vastzetten

Hier wordt het verschil tastbaar tussen het perspectief van een vriend nemen en het perspectief van een vriend krijgen. Nemen doe ik in mijn eigen hoofd, met het beeld dat ik al had. 1. ASML’s Reported 10% Increase in Replacement Parts Prices

October 10, 2026 · TheElec: ASML raises replacement parts prices

ASML is raising prices for replacement parts supplied to Samsung Electronics($005930.KS) and SK hynix($000660.KS) for DUV and EUV lithography systems by 10%, effective for deliveries from January 2027, according to the report. TheElec also reported that price increases for new systems were being negotiated separately. The account is based on industry reporting.

Parts inside a machine have different replacement cycles. Some need replacing while the machine itself still has years of useful life. Customers negotiate parts prices with ASML to keep existing machines running, as well as negotiating when they order new ones.

ASML sells lithography systems, which transfer circuit patterns using light. A wafer, the round disk on which many chips are made together, is coated with a light-sensitive material. The system exposes that material to light in the desired pattern.

Even if you have no plans to buy a new car, higher replacement parts prices raise your maintenance bill. A chip factory can similarly face higher parts costs for its existing lithography systems in a year when it orders no new ones.

From Selected Parts to a Blanket Increase

According to TheElec, ASML previously adjusted prices for selected parts when raw-material costs rose sharply or procurement became difficult. This time, the report described a blanket 10% increase for DUV and EUV replacement parts supplied in South Korea. ASML’s 2022 annual report also discusses sharing higher material, freight, and labor costs with customers. Negotiating to pass on costs is not new; the notable change in this report is the range of parts covered.

The same report cited industry accounts of tight equipment and parts supply as AI memory and foundry capacity expansions coincide. Customers trying to raise production cannot easily postpone purchases of parts needed to keep their machines running. If the report is accurate, ASML is using its existing bargaining power to apply price increases across a wider range of parts. How much that adds to profit, however, depends on both selling prices and procurement costs.

The Price Increase and the Actual Cost

Suppose the total annual cost of a process is 100, and purchases of the affected parts account for 5. If purchasing volumes stay the same and those parts become 10% more expensive, their cost rises to 5.5. Total cost increases from 100 to 100.5, or 0.5%.

The cost burden on customers depends on both the price increase and the affected parts’ share of total costs. Applying 10% to all of Samsung Electronics’ or SK hynix’s capital spending would exaggerate the effect.

The same applies on ASML’s side. Revenue from installed systems includes services and upgrades as well as parts. Applying a price increase for a specific category of purchases by Korean customers to worldwide installed-base revenue would inflate revenue that is not covered by the increase. If procurement costs have also risen, some of the higher selling price goes toward covering those costs.

The disclosed financial results for services and upgrades combine several categories and regions, making it difficult to isolate the profit effect of this increase. The change to watch is the broader range of parts subject to higher prices. Whether increases extend to other customers and regions will indicate how widely ASML is exercising that bargaining power.

2. Developing a Larger Mask for High-NA

September 8, 2026 · ASML and TSMC($TSM): joint development of larger masks


ASML and TSMC announced plans to develop larger masks, targeting a pilot line in 2031 and system readiness for leading-edge processes in 2033. An ASML and Intel($INTC) announcement on the same day specified a 6 × 12-inch format.

In the same announcement, TSMC said it expected to use High-NA in leading-edge volume production from 2030 and expand its use thereafter. Circuit devices and wiring are built in multiple layers, with light used to print the required pattern for each layer. The idea is to start with High-NA on layers requiring the finest patterning, then use it on more layers. Larger masks are intended to improve productivity after that initial adoption by increasing the area printed in one exposure. A major customer’s attention is shifting from testing equipment performance toward preparing for volume production.

The light-sensitive coating on a wafer reacts differently in exposed and unexposed areas. A mask is a plate that controls where light reaches the coating to form the circuit pattern. In DUV, it transmits or blocks light; in EUV, reflective and absorbing regions create the pattern. The lithography system reduces this image and transfers it onto the coating. Subsequent processing forms the actual circuit in the wafer.

The object being enlarged here is the mask. The round silicon wafer on which many chips are made is not getting bigger. The aim is to enlarge the region that can be printed in one exposure on the same wafer. That region is called the field. It can contain several small chips, or a single large chip can occupy most of it.

High-NA EUV uses larger mirrors to resolve finer patterns. Larger mirrors, however, increase the angles at which light strikes the mask, making it harder for the mask to reflect the light properly. ASML addressed this incidence-angle problem with optics that reduce the image more in one direction than the other. The circuit pattern on the mask is reduced to one-quarter of its size in one direction and one-eighth in the other.

Conventional EUV reduces the image to one-quarter in both directions. Because High-NA reduces it more in one direction, the printed field is half as long along that axis. With the other dimension unchanged, the area printed in one exposure is also halved. The maximum field goes from 26 × 33 mm to 26 × 16.5 mm.

Mask Size and Exposure Area

Moving from a 6 × 6-inch mask to a 6 × 12-inch mask doubles one side and the area. A longer circuit pattern along the direction with 8× reduction is intended to enlarge the field printed on the wafer.

If a large chip will not fit inside a smaller exposure field, its design must fit that field or the pattern must be exposed in sections whose boundaries are joined precisely. This joining of separately exposed patterns into a single circuit is called stitching. A larger mask and exposure field could ease those design and stitching requirements.

A larger mask changes the manufacturing requirements for the blank, its underlying material. A blank is a glass substrate coated with multiple films; it becomes a mask once the circuit pattern is fabricated on it. Flatness and film thickness must remain uniform across the larger plate, and defects must be controlled. Blank suppliers AGC($5201.T) and HOYA($7741.T) are relevant companies to follow.

DNP($7912.T) is among the mask makers that fabricate circuits on these blanks. DNP has announced the supply of masks for High-NA evaluation. IMS Nanofabrication supplies electron-beam mask-writing equipment, while Lasertec($6920.T) supplies inspection equipment that uses EUV wavelengths to find pattern defects. All need ways to handle a larger plate precisely. Having an existing High-NA product is not the same as having completed preparations for the 6 × 12-inch format.

Masks are reused across many wafers, rather than discarded after one use. Doubling their area therefore does not double sales volumes. The opportunity lies in making and inspecting larger plates without defects. Suppliers that can deliver reliable larger masks can compete for orders under the new format. Blank prototypes, mask-fabrication yields, and inspection equipment for the larger format will show how far preparations have progressed.

Equipment Prices and Cost per Chip

Customers want the ability to make many competitive chips more than they want an elaborate machine for its own sake. Suppose allocated equipment costs and operating costs over the same period rise from 100 to 110, while the number of good products rises from 100 to 120. Cost per product falls from 1 to about 0.92.

The denominator is the number of good products that can be sold. It depends on processing speed, uptime, and how many products are defective. Unlike the replacement parts price increase discussed earlier, new equipment can offer the possibility of producing a desired pattern with fewer steps or obtaining more good products.

For High-NA to spread in volume production, it needs to print fine patterns accurately while lowering cost per chip. TSMC’s stated sequence is to adopt it with existing masks, then improve productivity with larger ones. Changing the format for mask fabrication, inspection, and handling creates development needs beyond the lithography machine itself. More detail on the production processes and layers where TSMC will use High-NA, along with progress toward the larger-mask pilot schedule, will indicate how the plan is advancing.

3. Considering 8-High HBM amid Supply Constraints

September 29, 2026 · TrendForce: supply and cost constraints prompt consideration of 8-high HBM


TrendForce reported that GPU and custom AI chip designers were considering reducing HBM stack heights from 12 to 8 dies in some products. It attributed this to limited supply and system costs. This was not an announcement of finalized specifications for individual customers’ products.

You might expect a better AI chip to require taller memory stacks. Supply shortages can push the choice in the opposite direction. Customers may accept a little less memory in each system to ship more systems overall.

HBM consists of multiple DRAM chips, which temporarily store data, stacked and connected vertically through many electrical paths. One such group is called a stack. It exchanges large amounts of data close to the compute chip. The terms “8-high” and “12-high” refer to the number of DRAM dies in that stack.

Allocating 96 DRAM Dies

For illustration, suppose there are 96 good DRAM dies of equal capacity and no assembly losses. Stacking 12 at a time produces 8 HBM stacks; stacking 8 at a time produces 12. If the number of stacks per GPU stays the same, memory can be allocated to more GPUs. Each GPU, however, has less memory capacity.

Memory capacity and data-transfer speed also need to be distinguished. Reducing the number of stacked DRAM dies does not reduce the width of the connections and their operating speed in the same proportion. It does, however, leave less room for large models and working data. Customers must weigh the capacity their workloads need against the number of GPUs they can obtain.

A move to lower specifications can itself be a consequence of strong demand. When supply is constrained, customers may choose several systems with sufficient specifications over one with the highest specifications. If actual 8-high products launch and shipments expand, that would confirm a product-level choice to distribute scarce memory across more AI systems.

On October 11, Elon Musk also posted a brief reply on X: “Problem is RAM supply”. He did not specifically identify HBM. Achieving the desired AI performance and securing enough memory to supply that product widely are separate problems.

Assembly and Test Demand for 8-High HBM

A base die sits beneath the DRAM, connecting it to external circuitry. In the example above, increasing the number of stacks from 8 to 12 also increases the number of base dies from 8 to 12. Handling and testing operations performed once per completed stack may increase as well.

Workload changes differently depending on what a tool handles. Cutting and moving individual DRAM dies still involves 96 dies. If each finished HBM stack is tested individually, however, the number of test objects rises from 8 to 12. A 50% increase in stack count does not mean 50% more of every type of equipment is needed. Test time and spare capacity on existing tools also matter when estimating expansion needs.

The same distinction applies to cost. As TrendForce noted, a base die is still needed even when fewer DRAM dies are stacked. The purchase price of one stack may fall without the price per GB falling as well.

Shorter stacks can ease the pressure to make dies extremely thin. Warped or uneven dies are still difficult to bond, however. Applied Materials($AMAT) products announced on June 25 address precisely these issues: die warpage, bonding-surface flatness, and copper-plating uniformity.

If customers choose to produce more 8-high HBM using an existing process, they may buy more of their existing bonders while postponing the adoption of next-generation ones. Stack height alone cannot tell us the direction of equipment demand.

4. Making CoWoS Interposers and Assembling the Package

October 8, 2026 · GlobalFoundries($GFS): agreement to make silicon interposers for TSMC


GlobalFoundries agreed to manufacture silicon interposers for TSMC‘s CoWoS in the United States. It will expand capacity at its Malta, New York, facility, targeting the start of a production ramp in the first half of 2028.

“If GF is taking on CoWoS, isn’t it taking work away from Amkor($AMKR)?” That is a reasonable question after reading the headline. Both companies participate in advanced packaging. Under this agreement, however, GF’s job is to manufacture the interposer, the plate that connects the chips.

HBM stacks memory dies vertically. In CoWoS, completed HBM stacks and compute chips sit side by side on an interposer. They exchange data through its dense wiring. Making that plate and attaching chips to it to produce a finished package are different jobs.

Amkor announced an agreement with TSMC on June 16 for advanced packaging and testing services in the United States. GF’s interposer manufacturing and Amkor’s assembly and testing occupy different production stages.

Suppose an assembly line is waiting because interposers are in short supply. More interposers would allow the assembly provider to produce more finished packages. Capacity added at an earlier stage can support work at a later one. Competitive concerns would arise if GF also took on the same assembly and testing work and TSMC reduced the volume allocated to Amkor. The two disclosed agreements instead suggest a plan to secure both packaging components and assembly capacity in the United States.

Taken together, the announcements show TSMC securing component manufacturing separately from assembly and testing in the United States. GF’s expansion could relieve a shortage of interposers and help downstream shipments. How much of that becomes Amkor revenue depends on the products and volumes TSMC actually allocates to it.

Applied Materials supplies the processing equipment needed for this manufacturing work. It sells machines used to make the products, such as the HBM plating and planarization tools discussed earlier. The phrase “participating in CoWoS” therefore does not tell us where revenue comes from. We need to know whether a company supplies interposers, provides assembly services, or sells equipment to the factory.

Expanding advanced packaging involves more than adding an assembly line. Interposer production, assembly, and testing all need to expand for finished-product shipments to grow. The GF agreement is a concrete investment in securing those interposers in the United States. Equipment demand can arise at factories processing these components as well as at final assembly providers.

Copper Wiring and Plating Equipment

At its April 22 technology event, TSMC said it was producing CoWoS at 5.5 times the area of a conventional lithography field. More compute chips and HBM require more wiring area beneath them. This does not mean the lithography machine’s single-exposure area has grown.

Copper plating is one way to create that wiring. A patterned mold is formed over a thin metal layer, and copper grows in its openings. Removing the mold and the exposed thin metal layer leaves separate copper traces. If thickness differs between the center and edges of a large plate, subsequent connection steps become harder.

Applied’s May announcement of its NEXX acquisition concerns this work. It added plating equipment for large panels to its existing wafer-plating offering. The transaction closed on June 3. As the plates connecting chips grow larger, equipment that can process a large area at once becomes more valuable. The NEXX acquisition can be read as an investment in the plating capability needed as large AI package production expands from wafers to panels.

This manufacturing shift also connects to TSMC’s packaging expansion. ASE($ASX) announced development of a panel production line for AI and high-performance computing in May. Applied’s opportunity spans a shift toward larger formats by multiple manufacturers, rather than depending on one particular fab.

If interposers are ready but assembly is delayed, or vice versa, finished-product shipments must wait. That is why GF’s 2028 production schedule and Amkor’s factory start-up need to be tracked separately. Even a factory that starts first may be unable to run at sufficient volume while it waits for the next stage.
